blocks.text: Now we must state what الفنك [al-fanak] alphenec is, by which word we have said that other Arabs rendered the Hebrew שפן saphan. Gabriel Sionita, in Clim. 1, section 1 of the Geographia Nubiensis, translates it white weasel. Golius translates it hay-weasel, commonly fovina [beech marten] (because the most learned man thought that فنك [fanak] phenec alludes to foenum [hay], and that fovina [beech marten] is named from foenum [hay], whereas it has its name from the French word for beech). To Giggeius فنك [fanak] phenec is a certain most useful beast, from whose skin fur garments are obtained. But it is better to hear the Arabs themselves. Abenbitar: الفنك حر طيب الرايحة اطيب من جميع انواع الفرأء يجلب كثيرا [col. 1007] من الصقالبة ويشبه ان يكون في لحمه حلاوة وهو ابرد من السمور واحر من السنجاب واكثر الناس علي اختلاف اسنانهم يحتملون لبس الفنك [al-fanak ḥarr ṭayyib al-rāʾiḥa aṭyab min jamīʿ anwāʿ al-firāʾ yujlab kathīran min al-ṣaqāliba wa-yushbih an yakūn fī laḥmihi ḥalāwa wa-huwa abrad min al-sammūr wa-aḥarr min al-sinjāb wa-akthar al-nās ʿalā ikhtilāf asnānihim yaḥtamilūn lubs al-fanak] Phenec is an animal whose pelt is warm, of a good odor, the most fragrant among all kinds of furs. It is brought in great abundance from Secalia. It seems to be of sweet flesh. Its pelt is cooler than the pelt of τοῦ [tou] simor, but warmer than the pelt of τοῦ [tou] sungiab. It is customary to be clothed especially in this pelt as age advances. Razi: الفنك والقماقم والحواصل معتدلة في الحرارة وهو مع ذلك خفيفة [al-fanak wa-al-qamāqim wa-al-ḥawāṣil muʿtadila fī al-ḥarāra wa-huwa maʿa dhālika khafīfa] The pelts of alphenec, and alkamakim, and alhawasil, are of temperate warmth, and moreover light. Damir: الفنك دويبة يوخذ منها الفرو قال ابن البيطار انه اطيب من جميع الفراء يجلب كثيرا من بلاد الصقلاب [al-fanak duwaybba yuʾkhadh minhā al-farw qāla ibn al-bayṭār annahu aṭyab min jamīʿ al-firāʾ yujlab kathīran min bilād al-ṣaqlāb] Alphenec, a little animal from which fur is taken. Abenbitar said that it is the most fragrant of all furs, and is brought in great quantity from the Slavic region: which is how one should read above, not صقالية [ṣaqāliya] Secalia (the Slavic region, that is, of the Slavs, was formerly in European Scythia toward the Western Ocean, as Simocatta testifies in book 6, chapter 2). Ibnomar Ben Abdalbar, in the book entitled غهيد [ghhyd], that is, Explanation: الفنك والسنجاب والسمور كل ذلك سبع كالثعلب وابن عرس [al-fanak wa-al-sinjāb wa-al-sammūr kull dhālika sabʿ ka-al-thaʿlab wa-ibn ʿirs] Phenec, and sungiab, and simur are all wild beasts like the fox and the weasel. Thus they speak: from which it might seem to be gathered that these pelts are among the species of marten. Nevertheless الفنك [al-fanak] alphenec ra[?]

[II, 417] is the Pontic mouse, that is, a species of mouse or squirrel, which Hermolaus calls Venetian, and Agricola calls Finnish, from the Venedi and Finns, peoples by the Vistula in Prussia, by whom it is brought down to us for the use of furs. Concerning these peoples, Ptolemy writes thus in his description of Sarmatia: Παρὰ μὲν τὸν Οὐιστούλαν ποταμὸν ὑπὸ τοὺς Οὐενέδας Γύθωνες, εἶτα Φίννοι· [Para men ton Ouistoulan potamon hypo tous Ouenedas Gythōnes, eita Phinnoi·] Along the Vistula river, below the Venedi, are the Gythones, then the Finns. From these Finns, I say, the Finnish mouse seems to be named, and in Arabic فنك [fanak] phenec, which from its size and color is called by the French petigris ^{(4)}. Moreover, سنجاب [sinjāb] sungiab according to Golius is the squirrel, an animal of ash-gray color, and its pelt, with which garments are lined, or rather minium (he meant, I believe, herminium [ermine]). Damir says that it is an animal in the shape of a mole, larger than a mouse, living in the tops of trees, with a bluish, very soft, very beautiful pelt, in which luxurious people clothe themselves. It is evident that a species of squirrel is being described. Simur is also a kind of mouse, not altogether unknown to the Greeks. Hesychius: Σίμωρ παρὰ Πάρθοις καλεῖταί τι μυὸς ἀγρίου εἶδος, οὗ ταῖς δοραῖς [col. 1008] χρῶνται πρὸς χιτῶνας· [Simōr para Parthois kaleitai ti myos agriou eidos, hou tais dorais chrōntai pros chitōnas·] Among the Parthians a certain species of wild mouse is called Simor, whose skins are put to use for garments. To others simur is the marten. Damir says that it is an animal like a cat, or النمس [al-nims] a ferret, according to the opinion of some, whose pelt so excels in softness, lightness, warmth, and beauty that kings and magnates are clothed in it. Concerning either pelt I could add much more, drawn from the books of the Arabs; but to explain each of these matters more accurately is not for our leisure, nor does it contribute much to the present subject.
Among the Greeks there is an equal inconsistency in the explanation of the word שפן saphan.
1. There are some who render it λαγωοὺς [lagōous]; as the Vulgate translator has little hares: which we have already examined above.

2. There were some who preferred hyena; such as Clement of Alexandria in book 2 of the Paedagogus, chapter 10, where he introduces Moses as saying, Οὐκ ἔδεσαι τὸν λαγὼν, οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν [Ouk edesai ton lagōn, oude tēn hyainan], You shall not eat the hare, nor the hyena, that is, הארנבת והשפן. Similar to this is what is read in the Epistle of Barnabas: Ἀλλὰ καὶ δασύποδα οὐ φάγῃ [Alla kai dasypoda ou phagē], Moreover, you shall not eat the hare either. And a little later, Ἀλλὰ οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν φάγῃ [Alla oude tēn hyainan phagē], for which the old version has, Moreover, you shall not eat the beast either. I would prefer beluum [hyena], or belbum [hyena]. For thus writes Julius Capitolinus in the life of the third Gordian: There were under Gordian at Rome 32 elephants, 10 elks, 10 tigers, 60 tame lions, 30 tame leopards, [II, 418] 10 belbi, that is, hyenas. Nevertheless, in the Glossary, Philoxenus has: Ὕαινα· ζῶον [Hyaina· zōon], beast.
